spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2019 · General Studies Paper II · Q12
spec.text: “Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be enlarged into absolute power.” In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution by expanding its amending power ?

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty nineteen. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Can Parliament destroy the Constitution's basic structure by expanding its own amending power? Here's the strange part. Parliament once wrote a clause that tried to do exactly that.
scenes.visual: The printed question on a paper card, credit line 'UPSC CSE (Main) 2019, GS Paper II, Q12'. The words 'by expanding its amending power' glow faintly (plant).

spec.text: “Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be enlarged into absolute power.” In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution by expanding its amending power ?

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Explain whether means give a reasoned yes or no. And there are four jobs. Explain the statement. Show what Article three sixty-eight allows. Answer whether the power can grow. Then weigh it.
scenes.visual: Question X-ray: 'explain whether' highlighted; four empty boxes D1 to D4 (plant: they tick at the end).

lines: add, change or repeal any provision

lines.text: some changes: half the States too

scenes.vo: Start with the power itself. Article three sixty-eight lets Parliament add, change or repeal any provision. It needs a special majority in each House. Some changes also need half the States.
scenes.visual: Cartoon Parliament: a bill passing two doors, a two-thirds gauge, a row of State flags (no party symbols).

spec.title: THE AMENDING POWER AND ITS LIMIT

scenes.vo: But in nineteen seventy-three, thirteen judges sat in Kesavananda Bharati. By seven to six, they set a limit. The power to amend does not include the power to alter the basic structure.
scenes.visual: A long bench of thirteen chairs; the vote counter stops at 7 to 6.

spec.title: THE AMENDING POWER AND ITS LIMIT

scenes.vo: So in nineteen seventy-six, Parliament pushed back. The Forty-second Amendment added two clauses. One said no court could question any amendment. The other said there was no limit whatever on the power.
scenes.visual: The 1976 Gazette as a paper card; clauses 368(4) and 368(5) highlighted (pay-off of the plant).

spec.title: THE AMENDING POWER AND ITS LIMIT

items.what: Minerva Mills: both clauses struck down, 5 to 0

quote.text: The power to destroy is not a power to amend.

scenes.vo: But in nineteen eighty, in Minerva Mills, all five judges struck both clauses down. Their reason is the line in our question. A limited power cannot enlarge itself into an absolute one. The power to destroy is not a power to amend.
scenes.visual: The judgment as a quote card (Minerva Mills, 1980); the two clauses fade, still printed but marked invalid.

blocks.text: The statement echoes Minerva Mills (1980): a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot use it to make itself all-powerful.
1. The power under Article 368

• Parliament may amend 'by addition, variation or repeal any provision' (Art. 368(1)). • Special majority: a majority of each House's total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting; some federal provisions also need half the States. • Art. 368(3): Art. 13 does not apply to amendments.
2. Can it destroy the basic structure? No

• Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges, 7:6): the amending power does not include the power to alter the basic structure. • The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to expand it: Art. 368(4) barred courts from questioning any amendment, and 368(5) declared 'no limitation whatever'. • Minerva Mills (1980) struck both down 5:0: 'The power to destroy is not a power to amend.' • The test still bites: the 99th Amendment (NJAC) fell 4:1 in 2015; I.R. Coelho (2007) opened post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to review.
A timeline arrow: Art. 368 power → Kesavananda sets the limit (1973) → the 42nd Amendment adds 368(4)-(5) (1976) → Minerva Mills strikes them down (1980) → NJAC (2015).
blocks.label: Fig. 1: The limit, and the attempt to remove it

blocks.text: 3. Weighing it

Parliament can still amend any part within the limit; the judiciary decides whether it is crossed (NCERT), and what counts as basic is still debated. Change stays open: Ambedkar held that those who cannot win a two-thirds majority cannot claim the public's backing.
So Parliament can amend the Constitution but not unmake it: the limit guards its identity while keeping it open to change.

scenes.vo: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open by naming where the statement comes from. That one line shows you know the case.

scenes.vo: Section two answers the question directly: no. Then prove it in order. Kesavananda sets the limit. The Forty-second Amendment tries to remove it. Minerva Mills strikes that down. And it still applies: in twenty fifteen, the judicial appointments amendment fell four to one.

scenes.vo: Section three weighs it. Parliament can still amend any part, within the limit. The courts decide where the limit is. And Ambedkar's point keeps change open. Win two-thirds, and you can change the text, inside the limit.

weak.text: The basic structure is laid down in Article 368.
weak.miss: the words 'basic structure' appear nowhere in the Constitution

weak.text: Kesavananda Bharati gave a fixed list of the basic features.
weak.miss: NCERT itself says what counts as basic is still debated

weak.text: Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain was the first time an amendment was struck down.
weak.miss: a common belief the record does not support

weak.text: So Parliament can never amend Fundamental Rights.
weak.miss: wrong: it can amend any part within the limit

heads: 2. Can it destroy the basic structure? No

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It says the basic structure is written in the Constitution. It isn't. It says Kesavananda gave a fixed list. Even NCERT says that is debated. It repeats a common myth about Indira Gandhi's case. It says Fundamental Rights can never be amended. And it never mentions the two clauses the question is about.
